name: Facade
intent: Provide one simple interface to a complicated set of classes.
scenario: Starting a movie in a home theater means dimming lights, turning on the projector, setting the amplifier and pressing play, in the right order.
problem: A home theater has four components with their own APIs. Every place that starts a movie must call them all, in the correct order. Forget one step and you get sound with no picture.
solution: Create a HomeTheater facade with simple methods like watchMovie() and endMovie(). It knows the subsystems and the correct order. Clients call the facade and ignore the details. The subsystems are still available for people who need them.
pain: Every client repeats the same four-step recipe
Order matters and is easy to get wrong
Clients are coupled to every subsystem class
Changing the recipe means finding every copy
benefits: One call, watchMovie(), does it all
The correct order lives in one place
Clients depend on one class, not four
Subsystems stay usable directly when needed
whenToUse: You want a simple entry point to a complex subsystem or library
Several clients repeat the same multi-step workflow
You want to layer a system and limit coupling between layers
whenNotToUse: Clients need fine-grained control over every step
The facade would just forward calls without simplifying anything
pitfalls: A facade can grow into a god object that knows too much
It may hide features that some clients genuinely need
Becomes a dumping ground for unrelated convenience methods
Easy to confuse with Adapter: a facade simplifies, an adapter converts

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Calls the facade instead of the subsystem classes.

roles.label: Facade
roles.description: Simple interface that knows how to drive the subsystems.

roles.label: Subsystem classes
roles.description: The real components that do the work.

quiz.question: An order service calls the inventory, payment and shipping clients in that exact order. The same six-line sequence is copied into 7 controllers. A new fraud check must now run between payment and shipping. What is the best design change?
options: Wrap each of the three clients in an adapter so their method names and types match each other
Add the fraud check to the 7 controllers one by one and add a code review checklist item for it
Add an OrderFacade with a placeOrder method that runs the sequence, and have all 7 controllers call it
Make the 7 controllers inherit from a base controller that holds the three client instances
quiz.explanation: A facade puts the ordered workflow in one place, so the fraud check is added once. Adapters only convert interfaces, they do not remove the repeated recipe. A shared base class shares the clients but each controller would still repeat the sequence.

quiz.question: A video library facade offers convert(file, format) and hides codecs, bitrates and container settings. One team needs to set a custom bitrate per scene, and the facade cannot do that. What is the best response?
options: Let that team call the underlying subsystem classes directly, and keep the facade simple for everyone else
Add a bitrate, scene and codec parameter for each team's need to convert, so the facade covers every case
Make the subsystem classes private so all teams must go through the facade and request features there
Replace the facade with an adapter, because an adapter exposes all the subsystem options in one class
quiz.explanation: A facade is a convenience layer, and the subsystem stays available for clients who need fine control. Growing convert() to cover every option turns the facade into as complex as the subsystem it was meant to hide. An adapter converts interfaces, it does not expose more options.

quiz.question: A ReportingFacade started with 5 methods. Two years later it has 60 methods that touch billing, user accounts, email and exports, and every change to it causes merge conflicts. What is the most sensible fix?
options: Merge the billing, user, email and export classes into it so it owns their logic directly
Define an interface with all 60 methods so that the callers depend on an abstraction
Split it into several smaller facades, one for each area, each with a few workflow methods
Make it a singleton so that only one team at a time can change the shared instance
quiz.explanation: A facade that knows everything has become a god object. Smaller facades, one per area, keep each entry point simple and reduce conflicts. An interface with 60 methods hides nothing, and merging the subsystems in makes the problem worse.
